extracted.intended_audience: regulatory economists, policy analysts, and stakeholders commenting on the FTC non-compete rule (notice-and-comment participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) excerpt quantifying benefits and costs of the FTC final rule on non-competes over a ten-year horizon, including formulas, parameter values, and sensitivity analyses for earnings, innovation, prices, R&D, human-capital investment, and litigation/administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase in worker earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase in worker earnings = (% Increase in Earnings caused by the change in enforceability of non-competes) * (Total Affected Earnings). The Commission's primary estimate of the percent increase in workers' earnings is 0.86%. Total affected annual earnings are estimated to be $6.2 trillion (2023 dollars), producing an annual earnings effect of $53 billion and ten-year present discounted values reported in Table 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary approach requires no extrapolation (uses average magnitude change in enforceability from literature). The Commission multiplies a percent effect drawn from empirical studies by total affected earnings to estimate annual and ten-year effects (discounted at 2%, 3%, and 7%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis — full extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Full extrapolation calculates the effect on worker earnings by extrapolating to the effect of a complete prohibition on non-competes (enforceability score falls to zero). This yields a percent effect on earnings of 3.2%. Total affected earnings for this sensitivity are $7.3 trillion (2023 dollars), implying an annual earnings gain of $234 billion and ten-year discounted values in Table 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach scales the empirical effect to a larger change in enforceability than studied in the literature and may overstate effects; reported to show robustness to larger extrapolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis — partial extrapolation (to minimum observed enforceability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial extrapolation scales each State's empirical effect on earnings by the change required to bring its enforceability score down to the minimum observed enforceability score among States that do not broadly prohibit non-competes (0.53, New York). For each State, change in score is computed and used to scale literature estimates; affected earnings per State = State total earnings * estimated percent of covered workers (80%). Summing State results gives the national estimate (annual example: West Virginia: 0.64% * $0.24T = $152M). Resulting national annual estimate reported (e.g., $161 billion) and ten-year discounted values in Table 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More conservative than full extrapolation; explicitly demonstrates state-by-state scaling and aggregation; Commission notes this may still overestimate changes given recent state-level reductions in enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers versus benefits (treatment in RIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish earnings gains that are transfers (a gain for one group and an equal-dollar loss for another) from earnings that represent net social benefits (higher productivity/allocative efficiency). Transfers are not net benefits in regulatory impact analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because literature cannot fully separate transfers versus benefits, Commission examines evidence of external effects (spillovers, effects on neighboring states, effects on workers without non-competes) and conducts scenario analyses that allocate varying percentages of earnings effects to benefits (see Part X.F.10). The RIA documents evidence supporting some market-level benefits (e.g., external effects estimated at 76% on neighboring-state workers; wage effects for non-bound workers in same industry/state), but retains sensitivity to uncertainty by varying the assumed benefit share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation — change in patenting (quantity and quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase in # of Patents = (% Increase in Patenting) * (Total # of Affected Patents). Commission estimates percent increase in patenting due to an average magnitude enforceability change to be 10.9%–18.7% annually over ten years, phasing in from about 2.0%–3.4% in year 1 to 19.8%–34.0% in year 10. Total number of affected patents each year is taken as 156,976. Resulting additional patent counts per year are reported in Table 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission does not monetize patents because no reliable estimate of the social value of a patent exists; uses citation-weighted patents and other quality measures to note that quality (not just quantity) increases when non-competes are less enforceable. Performs state-level partial extrapolation analogous to earnings and reports sensitivity ranges (extrapolated columns in Table 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation — R&D spending change
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction in R&D Spending = (% Reduction in Spending) * (Total Affected Spending). Commission estimates % reduction in spending of 0–8.1%; total affected spending is $575 billion (2023 dollars), yielding an overall annual reduction of $0–$47 billion (2023 dollars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction in firm-level R&D represents cost savings for incumbents but may not reflect market-level effects because new firms might increase R&D; Commission therefore stops short of classifying R&D spending reductions as a social benefit. Empirical estimates are based on incumbent firms and may understate market-level innovation from new firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prices — effect on physician and clinical services (proxy for consumer price effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decrease in Prices = (% Decrease in Prices) * (Total Affected Spending). Based on the empirical study in healthcare, Commission estimates a 3.5% decrease in physician service prices. Total physician and clinical services spending (excluding States that broadly do not enforce non-competes) is $801 billion (2023 dollars). Commission applies coverage multipliers (35%, 61.9%, 75%) as proxies for spending under Commission jurisdiction and reports ten-year present value reductions in spending for physician/clinical services (Table 4: ranges such as $74–$194 billion depending on discount rate and coverage assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission treats price evidence as corroborating rather than unique because prices can reflect changes already measured elsewhere (innovation, investment, wages). Performs state-level partial extrapolation analogous to other outcomes (example: West Virginia price decrease 2.5%). Notes possible transfers from firms to consumers and that evidence is limited to healthcare, so extrapolation to other industries is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of the final rule — legal, administrative, litigation, and uncertain classification of human-capital effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds costs associated with the final rule, including legal and administrative costs, and possibly costs related to investment in human capital and litigation. It notes uncertainty whether human-capital changes are costs or benefits and whether litigation costs would rise or fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs are summarized in Table 1 (Part X.E). The analysis includes these effects in the RIA but recognizes substantial uncertainty and overlap across categories (e.g., training effects may already be reflected in wage estimates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in human capital — core training scenario (calculation of benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of Decreased Investment in Core Training = Additional Output of Workers Resulting From Less Time Spent Training + Reduced Direct Outlays on Training. Additional output = (Total # of Affected Workers) * (Percentage Point Decrease in Trained Workers) * (Average Hours Spent Training Per Worker) * (Average Hourly Output of Workers). Reduced Direct Outlays = [(Total Direct Outlays)/(# of Workers Receiving Training)] * [(Total # of Affected Workers) * (Percentage Point Decrease in Trained Workers)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters used: total affected workers = 101.1 million (if all workers) or 45.3 million (if only high-use occupations); percentage point decrease in trained workers = 0.4; average hours training per worker = 85; average hourly output = $60.77; total direct outlays on human capital = $105 billion; estimated # workers receiving training = 23.5 million. These calculations yield annual direct output and outlay savings (e.g., $1.9B in additional output + $1.6B reduced outlays under all-workers assumption). Ten-year discounted estimates assuming core training produce net benefits (Table 5: e.g., $32B at 2% discount assuming all occupations affected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in human capital — advanced training scenario (calculation of costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of Decreased Investment in Advanced Training = Additional Output of Workers Resulting From Less Time Spent Training + Reduced Direct Outlays on Training − Lost Output Resulting From Foregone Advanced Training. Lost output = (Total # of Affected Workers) * (Percentage Point Decrease in Trained Workers) * (Average Hourly Output of Workers) * (Average Hours Worked per Year) * (% Productivity Loss), with multi-year depreciation of returns to advanced training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters used: total affected workers = 101.1M or 45.3M; percentage point decrease = 0.4; average hourly output = $60.77; avg hours worked per year = 1,784; % productivity loss assumed = 6.4%; returns to training depreciate 20% per year. Commission models forgone advanced training each year through year ten, depreciates prior years' returns, and sums losses. Under advanced-training assumption, ten-year discounted effects are net costs (Table 5: e.g., −$41B at 2% discount assuming all occupations affected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of senior executives in estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Many estimates do not separately account for senior executives who may continue to work under non-competes under the rule. If senior executives remain bound by non-competes, some effects (e.g., earnings, innovation, prices) may be pushed into the future and thus be more heavily discounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission notes senior executives' earnings are a small share of total earnings (e.g., Chief Executives comprise ~0.5% of all earnings) so omission has limited impact overall, but it flags this as a source of timing/discounting uncertainty in multiple effect estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical literature and state-level scaling/aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission aligns chosen empirical estimates with metrics outlined elsewhere (Part IV.A.2) and adjusts findings from studies by the average magnitude change in enforceability (primary approach) or scales study estimates by state-specific enforceability-score changes for extrapolation approaches. For each outcome (earnings, patents, prices, spending), percent effect estimates from literature are multiplied by state-specific totals (earnings, patents, spending) and aggregated nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: adjust an occupation/industry comparison study to the average magnitude enforceability change (resulting in a 0.5% earnings effect in one study); compute state-specific percent changes (e.g., West Virginia 0.06 decrease in score => 0.64% earnings effect) then multiply by state totals and sum. Commission cautions that extrapolation may overstate effects as many States have already reduced enforceability.
